source_text: Qlnd quoque necessarie monet Dominus ut in oratione dicamus: et ne patiaris nos induci in temptationem. qua in parte ostenditur nihil contra nos aduersarium posse, nisi Deus ante permiserit, ut omnis timor noster et deuotio adque obseruatio ad Deum conuertatur, quando in temptationibus nihil malo liceat, nisi potestas inde tribuatur. probat scriptura quae dicit: uenit Nabuchodonosor rex Babyloniae in Hierusalem et expugnabat eam, et dedit eam Dominus in manu eius. datur autem potestas aduersum nos malo secundum nostra peccata, sicut scriptum est: quis dedit in direptionem Iacob et Israel eis qui praedabantur illum? nonne Deus cui peccauerunt et nolebant in uiis eius ambulare neque audire legem eius, et superduxit super eos iram animationis suae? et iterum Salomone peccante et a praeceptis adque a uiis Domini recedente positum est: et excitauit Dominus Satanan ipsi Salomoni.
thought_title: God's permission is required before the adversary can act
orientation: Cyprian is explaining the petition 'and do not allow us to be led into temptation' from the Lord's Prayer, showing that the devil has no power over us unless God permits it.
pass_a_gloss: And also necessarily [he] warns [the] Lord that in prayer we say: and [do] not [you] allow us to be led into temptation. in which part [it] is shown nothing against us [the] adversary [is] able, unless God before [has] permitted, so that all fear our and devotion and observance to God [may] be turned, when in temptations nothing to [the] evil [one] [is] allowed, unless power from there [is] granted. [it] proves [the] scripture which says: came Nabuchodonosor king of Babylonia into Jerusalem and was attacking it, and gave it [the] Lord into [the] hand of him. [it] is given however power against us to [the] evil [one] according to our sins, as [it] is written: who gave into plunder Jacob and Israel to those who were plundering him? not God to whom they sinned and they were not willing in [the] ways of him to walk nor to hear [the] law of him, and he brought over upon them [the] wrath of [the] spirit of him? and again Solomon sinning and from [the] precepts and from [the] ways of [the] Lord departing [it] was set down: and [he] stirred up [the] Lord Satan against Solomon himself.

choices.term: ne patiaris nos induci in temptationem
choices.english: and do not allow us to be led into temptation
choices.why: Literal rendering of the petition, preserving the passive infinitive and the negative command
rejected: and lead us not into temptation

choices.english: the adversary can do nothing against us
choices.why: Keeps the accusative-infinitive construction with 'adversarium' as subject of 'posse'
rejected: nothing can be done against us by the adversary

choices.english: unless God has first permitted it
choices.why: Preserves the temporal force of 'ante' and the perfect subjunctive
Keeps the passive voice and the source 'inde' referring to God

choices.term: et excitavit Dominus Satanan ipsi Salomoni
choices.english: and the Lord stirred up Satan against Solomon himself
choices.why: Literal rendering of the Hebrew-influenced construction with dative 'ipsi Salomoni'
rejected: and the Lord raised up an adversary against Solomon

bible_refs.note: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and was fighting against it, and the Lord gave it into his hand

who gave Jacob to plundering and Israel to those who were plundering him? Was it not God, against whom they sinned and were unwilling to walk in his ways nor to hear his law, and he brought upon them the wrath of his anger
and the Lord stirred up Satan against Solomon himself

pass_b_english: Here too the Lord gives us a necessary command for our prayer: “And do not allow us to be led into temptation.” In this petition he shows that the adversary can do nothing against us unless God has first permitted it, so that all our fear, devotion, and watchfulness may be turned toward God, since in temptations evil is allowed no power unless power from there is granted. Scripture proves this when it says: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and was fighting against it, and the Lord gave it into his hand (2 Kings 25:1; cf. Jeremiah 52:4). But power against us is granted to evil according to our sins, as it is written: Who gave Jacob to plundering and Israel to those who were plundering him? Was it not God, against whom they sinned and were unwilling to walk in his ways or hear his law, and he brought upon them the fury of his soul (Isaiah 42:24)? And again, when Solomon sinned and departed from the Lord’s commands and ways, it is written: And the Lord stirred up Satan against Solomon himself (1 Kings 11:14).

problems.source_quote: uenit Nabuchodonosor rex Babyloniae in Hierusalem et expugnabat eam, et dedit eam Dominus in manu eius
problems.why: Citation is 2 Kings 25:1 / Jeremiah 52:4 overlap, but text matches 2 Kings 25:1-2 more closely; Jeremiah 52:4 lacks 'expugnabat eam' sequence. Better cited as 2 Kings 25:1 or Jeremiah 52:4-5.
'Iram animationis suae' means 'wrath of his soul/spirit' or 'fierce wrath,' not 'wrath of his anger' which is tautological and misreads 'animationis'.
problems.ruling: 'animationis suae' = 'of his soul/spirit'; 'wrath of his anger' mistranslates and creates tautology.

fixed: Citation corrected to 2 Kings 25:1 with cross-reference to Jeremiah 52:4, since the source text matches 2 Kings 25:1-2 more closely.
Changed 'the wrath of his anger' to 'the fury of his soul' to render 'iram animationis suae' accurately.

last_rejected.why: expugnabat means 'besieged/conquered', not 'was fighting against'. Weakens the sense of successful assault.
last_rejected.ruling: expugnabat is imperfect of expugnare, meaning 'to assault/attack'; 'was fighting against' captures ongoing military action, within normal range.

last_rejected.source_quote: uenit Nabuchodonosor rex Babyloniae in Hierusalem et expugnabat eam, et dedit eam Dominus in manu eius
last_rejected.why: The citation should be 2 Kings/2 Samuel 24:1 or 1 Chronicles 21:1, not 2 Kings 25:1 or Jeremiah 52:4. The source text quotes about Nebuchadnezzar coming against Jerusalem, but the biblical parallel for God giving permission to the adversary is the David census narrative (2 Sam 24:1 / 1 Chr 21:1), where Satan/inciting spirit moves against Israel with God's permission. The English cites the wrong chapter and verse entirely.
last_rejected.ruling: Source quotes Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kgs 25/Jer 52), not David census. Citation matches source correctly.

last_rejected.quote: since in temptations evil is allowed no power unless power from there is granted
last_rejected.source_quote: quando in temptationibus nihil malo liceat, nisi potestas inde tribuatur
last_rejected.why: "inde" refers to God, not "from there" vaguely. The sense is "unless power is granted from him [God]." The English obscures that God is the one granting the power.
last_rejected.fix: since in temptations evil is allowed no power unless power is granted by him
last_rejected.ruling: 'inde' means 'from there/that source,' a standard rendering; meaning is preserved without forcing a pronoun.

last_rejected.source_quote: uenit Nabuchodonosor rex Babyloniae in Hierusalem et expugnabat eam, et dedit eam Dominus in manu eius
last_rejected.why: Those verses lack God giving the city into his hand. The wording is Daniel 1:1–2.
last_rejected.fix: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and was fighting against it, and the Lord gave it into his hand (Daniel 1:1–2).
last_rejected.ruling: The source quotes Nabuchodonosor coming to Jerusalem, 'dedit eam Dominus in manu eius'; Daniel 1:1–2 fits, but the cited 2 Kings 25:1 with 'cf.' is only a mislabeled reference. Still, it misdirects readers.
